flags: pour-into: entry-85 prints the supine “infūsum” without the long ī of its own īnfundō, īnfūdī (and of entry-249’s īnfūsum, īnfūsī n.); copied as printed.

entry-125’s heading printed “īnfūndō” with a long ū, against its own text (“the root vowel in fundō remains short”) and Lewis & Short (in-fundo, fūdi, fūsum); the heading is not carried over, and pour-into follows the body’s īnfundō.

piece, chop, bread, half: frūstum and frūstulum are printed with a long ū (entries 82, 84, 121, 123, 130, citing Bennett and Lewis’s Elementary), but the series spelling in latinitas AGENTS.md §2 is “frustum”, and entries 255 and 272 (culina-2) print frustātim. Which spelling should the lexicon follow?

wipe: the lemma “extergō, extergere” is Lewis & Short’s third-conjugation variant, cited only from the Vulgate and the Digest; the classical verb is extergeō, extergēre (Cato, Plaut.), which the example’s extergeāmus follows. Likewise the example “mēnsam tergāmus” (entry-85) uses the rarer tergō, while the lemma is tergeō, tergēre.
utensil: Lewis & Short gives ūtensilis as a noun only in the plural (ūtensilia); the singular “ūtēnsile, ūtēnsilis n.” is the card’s.
pulp: period kept post-classical as the card says, though Lewis & Short also cites Scribonius Largus (1st c.) for fruit pulp.

coffee: coffea stays recommended (“the headword coffea stands”), but the card calls caffēa “our preferred alternative in speech”, spells espresso and cappuccino “with caffēa as the lexicon prefers” (against Traupman 310 caffea expressa and M-O cafēa expressa), and the libellī write caffea (Libellus II, caffeae pōcillum). One spelling may want a ruling.
freezer: arca gelātōria leads, as on the card, though capsa frīgorifica is “the word of the libellī” (cf. pyjamas, where Jack chose the household word).
kitchen-knife: the card says only “recorded in both modern references”, but Lewis & Short (s.v. coquīnārius: culter coquīnāris, Varr. ap. Non.) and M-O (Varr.) attest it, so its period is classical.

Notes added from the cards’ own explanations: jentāculum and jentō (ruling jentaculum), lac (against Lewis’s Elementary lāc), fervefaciō (short e), īnfundō (long ī before nf), and the word rulings fork and gelatum.

cooking-pot: ōlla is added as an alternative without a note, since the card gives none; the olla ruling applies (saucepan cites it). culina-2’s entry-251 also gives ōlla “pot”, so both batches may extend cooking-pot.

Periods where the card is silent or vague: distill and distillation (“later technical use”) set to modern; ahēnum ēlectricum, pōculum ānsātum (M-O s.v. drink: cup), in frīgidārium pōnere/servāre, cistella merendae, īnstrūmenta culīnāria (the card’s heading) and pānis tostus (not in Lewis & Short) set to modern; conterō in the blender sense set to modern (“a modern application”); the descriptive cutting phrases of entry-123 set to ours, since the card calls that phrasing ours.
bag and kind: the cards cite no source for saccus or genus, so these records carry a one-line note instead.
have-lunch: “Venīte, prandēte!” is cited as Jo. 21, 12; the card’s “quoted in Libellus III” is kept in the evidence of prandeō, because check_libelli.py reads a phrase’s source as a single citation.

Examples that the cards printed together were split where each part illustrates a different word (e.g. “Pōma lavā. Urceum ēlue.”, “Incīsōrium ligneum; pōculum vitreum; culter ferreus”, “Aquam mētīre; nucēs pende.”).

thick and thin: crassus and tenuis come from the card’s note (“Crassus/tenuis describe consistency”) and its Lewis & Short links; dulcis, acidus and amārus stay in the smoothie comment, since sweet, sour and bitter are terms of entry-268 (culina-2).
Small edits: “Theo’s naming game” became “a naming game” (no names outside examples); Italian gelato is marked as <em>, not as Latin.

Overlaps with culina-2: bottle (entry-260 lagoena), dessert (entry-298 bellāria), freezer and toast (entry-272; also a drinking toast in entry-410), cup (pōcillum, entry-272), small dish/plate (entry-258 patella; the libellī use catillus), hearth/stove (entry-256 foculus, entry-415), oven, dice (entry-405 tessellātim concīdere, Apicius), chop finely (entry-405 minūtim concīdere), roast (entry-402 assum), be hungry (entry-261), flavour and taste (entry-408), blender (entry-415 māchina mīxtōria, with a long ī, against the provisional mixtus ruling that entry-117 follows), cheese pastry (entry-253 placenta), lunch (crūs, pectus: entry-252).

Overlaps with other categories: storeroom (entry-427), sponge, soap, cloth/towel and dry (entry-64), wipe (entry-91), rinse (entry-65), hearth (entry-270), cloth (entry-319, fabric), button (entry-62; this record has the sense “a control to press”), fill (entry-181), freeze (entry-502), cook (entry-545, the person), cut (entry-303, a wound), honey and herbal tea (entry-300), vitamin (entry-12), grind and squeeze out (entry-168), dice (entry-526, the game; this record has a sense), choose (entry-79; the example sits in pear).

Domain: kept as culina, though these plainly belong elsewhere: kind, part, minute, second, measure, weigh, weight, shopping list, wood, glass (material), steel, plastic, tool, sponge, soap, cloth, chest, storeroom, strength, and the general verbs make smaller, break into pieces, put, remove, take out, transfer, fill, press, keep and store.
